78746.e: The hourglass and the calendar show that a lot of time passes until the claim disappears. After a certain period, a claim or an offence can no longer be pursued; this is called the statute of limitations.
78746.m: Once the limitation period has passed, a claim can no longer be enforced.

78747.q: Which legal term do these pictures stand for?
a: Right to exclude others from your home
78747.e: Folders with information about a person are protected by a lock and a shield. Data protection rules how personal data may be handled; in Switzerland the revised Data Protection Act has applied since 2023.
78747.m: Data protection protects people from misuse of their personal data.

78748.q: Which legal term do these pictures stand for?
78748.e: Someone is not happy with a verdict (thumbs down) and goes to the next higher court. This legal remedy is called an appeal.
78748.m: With an appeal, you have a higher court review a verdict.

78749.q: Which legal term do these pictures stand for?
78749.e: The 18th birthday, the signature and the scales show that from the age of 18 you may sign contracts yourself. In Switzerland the age of majority has been 18 since 1996.
78749.m: Once you come of age, you may sign contracts on your own.

78750.q: Which legal term do these pictures stand for?
78750.e: A speaking head, a speech bubble, an open lock and scales stand for the right to express your opinion freely. Freedom of expression is guaranteed in Art. 16 of the Federal Constitution.
78750.m: Freedom of expression allows you to say your opinion openly.

78751.q: Which legal term do these pictures stand for?
78751.e: After an accident the car is repaired and the loss is made good with money, as the court decides. Anyone who unlawfully causes damage to another person must pay damages (Art. 41 of the Code of Obligations).
78751.m: Anyone who unlawfully causes damage to someone must pay damages.

78752.q: Which philosophical term do these pictures stand for?
78752.e: The zero in front of the universe and the shrug mean that nothing has a fixed meaning or value. This attitude is called nihilism (Latin nihil, nothing); Friedrich Nietzsche dealt with it intensively.
78752.m: Nihilism denies that there are fixed values or a meaning.

78753.q: Which philosophical term do these pictures stand for?
78753.e: Gold, a rule book, a handshake and the double arrow stand for a rule that works in both directions. The Golden Rule roughly says: treat others as you want to be treated yourself.
78753.m: The Golden Rule asks you to treat others as you would like to be treated.

78754.q: Which saying of an ancient philosopher do these pictures stand for?
a: “Man is the measure of all things”
78754.e: A bearded thinker points to his brain, shrugs and holds up a zero. The saying is attributed to Socrates and expresses that recognising your own ignorance is the beginning of wisdom.
78754.m: Socrates saw knowing your own ignorance as the beginning of wisdom.

78755.q: Which philosophical term do these pictures stand for?
78755.e: Eyes, ears, nose and hand lead to the brain: knowledge comes from sense experience. This teaching is called empiricism; an important representative was John Locke.
78755.m: Empiricism sees sense experience as the source of all knowledge.

78756.q: Which philosophical term do these pictures stand for?
78756.e: A body, the sign for two and a mind show that a human being consists of two substances. René Descartes held this mind-body dualism.
78756.m: Dualism distinguishes between body and mind as two separate substances.

78757.q: Which philosophical term do these pictures stand for?
78757.e: Many happy faces, a plus and numbers stand for the greatest happiness of the greatest number. According to the utilitarianism of Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, the good action is the one that maximises overall benefit.
78757.m: Utilitarianism judges actions by their benefit for as many people as possible.

78758.q: Which philosophical paradox do these pictures stand for?
78758.e: A runner, a tortoise, a finishing line and the infinity sign point to Zeno of Elea: swift Achilles seems never to catch the tortoise, because he would have to cover infinitely many stretches.
78758.m: Zeno’s paradox of Achilles and the tortoise plays with infinitely many stretches.

78759.q: Which philosophical thought experiment do these pictures stand for?
78759.e: All the wooden parts of a ship are replaced one by one, and the question is whether it is still the same ship. Plutarch passed down this thought experiment about identity.
78759.m: The Ship of Theseus asks whether something is still the same after all its parts are replaced.

78760.q: Which psychology term do these pictures stand for?
78760.e: Several groups point at a single, stressed person. Peer pressure arises when someone feels pushed to adapt to a group’s behaviour.
78760.m: Peer pressure can make people act against their own opinion.

78762.q: Which psychology term do these pictures stand for?
78762.e: A climber is completely relaxed and absorbed in what she is doing, time flies and everything flows like a wave. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi called this state of complete absorption flow.
78762.m: In flow you are so absorbed that you forget the time.

78763.q: Which psychology term do these pictures stand for?
78763.e: A briefcase, a flame, a candle and an exhausted face show that someone is burnt out inside from work. This state of deep exhaustion is called burnout.
78763.m: Burnout is a state of deep exhaustion from long overload.

78764.q: Which term from psychology do these pictures mean?
78764.e: Sun and a thought bubble with a sleepy face make day and dream. In a daydream, your thoughts wander while you are awake.
78764.m: In a daydream, your thoughts wander even though you are awake.

78765.q: Which psychology term do these pictures stand for?
78765.e: A house, a broken heart and a suitcase show someone far away who misses their home. This feeling is called homesickness; it was once considered a typical “Swiss illness”.
78765.m: Homesickness is longing for home when you are far away.

78766.q: Which psychology term do these pictures stand for?
78766.e: A brain, a stopwatch and a note flying away show that information is kept only briefly. According to George A. Miller, short-term memory stores about seven items for a short time.
78766.m: Short-term memory keeps only a little information for a short time.

78767.q: Which psychology term do these pictures stand for?
78767.e: A person reads quietly alone at home with the sound switched off. Introversion describes people who tend to recharge their energy in peace and alone; the term goes back to Carl Gustav Jung.
78767.m: Introverted people tend to recharge their energy in peace and alone.

78768.q: Which ecology term do these pictures stand for?
78768.e: A plant, a caterpillar, a bird and an eagle stand in a row in which each living thing is eaten by the next. Such a linear sequence of feeding relationships is called a food chain.
78768.m: In a food chain, each link is food for the next.

78769.q: Which ecology term do these pictures stand for?
78769.e: A butterfly, frog, mushroom, ladybird, hedgehog and plant show many different living things. The variety of species, genes and habitats is called biodiversity.
78769.m: Biodiversity means the variety of life on Earth.

78770.q: Which ecology term do these pictures stand for?
78770.e: Only maize grows on the whole field, one plant next to the other. Growing a single crop over a large area is called monoculture.
78770.m: In a monoculture only one single plant species is grown on an area.

78771.q: Which ecology term do these pictures stand for?
78771.e: A banana skin and carrots are broken down by worms, and a new plant grows from them. In composting, small creatures break down plant remains into nutrient-rich soil.
78771.m: Composting turns plant remains into fertile soil.

78772.q: Which ecology term do these pictures stand for?
78772.e: A bee carries pollen from one flower to the next. This transfer of pollen is called pollination and is needed so that many plants can form fruit.
78772.m: In pollination, pollen reaches the stigma of a flower.

78773.q: Which ecology term do these pictures stand for?
78773.e: A lamp lights up the city at night so brightly that you can no longer see the stars and nocturnal animals like the owl are disturbed. This brightening of the night sky by artificial light is called light pollution.
78773.m: Light pollution disturbs nocturnal animals and hides the starry sky.

78774.q: Which ecology term do these pictures stand for?
78774.e: Factory fumes form clouds from which rain falls that damages trees. Sulphur and nitrogen oxides make the rain acidic; in the 1980s this was part of the debate about “dying forests”.
78774.m: Acid rain forms when exhaust gases combine with water in the air to make acids.

78775.q: Which ecology term do these pictures stand for?
78775.e: A fishing boat with a net catches so many fish that their numbers fall. When more fish are caught than can grow back, it is called overfishing.
78775.m: Overfishing means more fish are caught than can grow back.

78776.q: Which term from the digital world do these pictures stand for?
78776.e: Lots of emails that go straight into the bin stand for unwanted mass messages. Such messages are called spam.
78776.m: Spam is unwanted mass email that usually ends up in the bin.

78777.q: Which term from the digital world do these pictures stand for?
78777.e: A key (password) plus a mobile phone with a number code lead to access. With two-factor authentication you need two independent proofs to log in.
78777.m: Two-factor authentication protects accounts with a second proof.

78778.q: Which term from the digital world do these pictures mean?
78778.e: A screen (mobile and computer) is photographed. A photo of the screen is called a screenshot.
78778.m: With a screenshot, you save a picture of the screen.

78779.q: Which term from the digital world do these pictures stand for?
78779.e: A person takes a selfie, lots of people follow them, and their reach grows. Someone who has many followers on social media and influences their opinions or shopping habits is called an influencer.
78779.m: Influencers use their reach on social media to influence many people.

78780.q: Which term from the digital world do these pictures stand for?
78780.e: A film plays over the internet straight away, like a flowing stream. With streaming, video or music is transmitted and played at the same time, without being fully downloaded first.
78780.m: With streaming, a film plays while it is still being transmitted.

78781.q: Which term from the digital world do these pictures stand for?
78781.e: A robot with a brain has an idea. Computer systems that solve tasks which would otherwise need human intelligence are called artificial intelligence (AI).
78781.m: Artificial intelligence lets computers solve tasks that require thinking.

78782.q: Which term from the digital world do these pictures stand for?
78782.e: A headset, a globe and a game controller stand for diving into a computer-generated world. With a VR headset you experience virtual reality.
78782.m: With a VR headset you dive into a virtual reality.

78783.q: Which term from the digital world do these pictures stand for?
78783.e: A crossed-out mobile phone, a tree and a person meditating show a deliberate break from digital devices. This time out is called a digital detox.
78783.m: In a digital detox you deliberately do without digital devices for a while.

78784.q: Which term from the digital world do these pictures stand for?
78784.e: A floppy disk and two identical folders show that files are copied and saved. Such a safety copy is called a backup.
78784.m: A backup is a safety copy that protects against data loss.

78785.q: Which linguistics term do these pictures stand for?
78785.e: Two different words (A and B) point to the same thing, such as bike and bicycle. Words with the same or a very similar meaning are called synonyms.
78785.m: Synonyms are different words with the same or a similar meaning.

78786.q: Which linguistics term do these pictures stand for?
78786.e: Mountains, a speaking head and a village stand for a form of language tied to a region. Such a regional variety of a language is called a dialect, for example Bernese German or Valais German.
78786.m: A dialect is a regional form of a language.

78788.q: Which linguistics term do these pictures stand for?
78788.e: A word comes in from the wider world and becomes at home in your own language. A loanword is taken from another language and adapted, for example the German word “Fenster” (window) from Latin fenestra.
78788.m: A loanword comes from another language but feels native.

78789.q: Which linguistics term do these pictures stand for?
78789.e: The sign for new, letters and a speech bubble show a newly created word. Newly created words such as “to google” are called neologisms.
78789.m: A neologism is a newly created word.

78790.q: Which term from linguistics do these pictures mean?
78790.e: Hands and hand signs replace the spoken word. Deaf people communicate with sign language; in Switzerland there are three sign languages.
78790.m: Sign languages are full languages that work with the hands, the face and the body.

78791.q: Which linguistics term do these pictures stand for?
78791.e: A word, a family tree, a clock and a magnifying glass show that the origin and history of a word are being studied. This discipline is called etymology.
78791.m: Etymology studies the origin and history of words.

78792.q: Which linguistics term do these pictures stand for?
78792.e: A mouth, a loudspeaker and a microscope show that speech sounds are studied closely. The science of how sounds are produced and perceived is called phonetics.
78792.m: Phonetics studies how speech sounds are made and heard.

78793.q: Which invention do these pictures stand for?
78793.e: A device that lets you see the moon enlarged from far away. A patent for the telescope was applied for in the Netherlands in 1608; Galileo Galilei pointed it at the sky in 1609.
78793.m: From the 17th century, the telescope let people observe distant celestial bodies.

78794.q: Which invention do these pictures stand for?
78794.e: Fire heats air, which lifts a balloon into the clouds. In 1783 the Montgolfier brothers launched the first crewed hot-air balloon in France.
78794.m: A hot-air balloon rises because warm air is lighter than cold air.

78795.q: Which invention do these pictures stand for?
78795.e: A cow, a syringe and a protective shield: in 1796 Edward Jenner transferred harmless cowpox to protect against dangerous smallpox. The word vaccine comes from Latin vacca, cow.
78795.m: Edward Jenner’s smallpox vaccination was the first scientific vaccination.

78796.q: Which invention do these pictures stand for?
78796.e: Light and writing make a picture: photography means “drawing with light” in Greek. Joseph Nicéphore Niépce made the oldest surviving photograph around 1826.
78796.m: The word photography means “drawing with light”.

78797.q: Which invention do these pictures stand for?
78797.e: In a factory, cars move one after another from station to station. In 1913 Henry Ford introduced the assembly line in car production and greatly lowered costs.
78797.m: The assembly line made cars cheaper through fast mass production.

78798.q: Which invention do these pictures stand for?
78798.e: Cold and a box with milk show a device that keeps food fresh. In the 1870s Carl von Linde developed a refrigerating machine that became the basis of the modern fridge.
78798.m: The fridge keeps food fresh for longer by cooling it.

78799.q: Which invention do these pictures stand for?
78799.e: Two brothers, a small propeller plane and sand dunes point to Orville and Wilbur Wright. In 1903 at Kitty Hawk they flew the first controlled powered aeroplane.
78799.m: The Wright brothers flew the first controlled powered aeroplane in 1903.

78800.q: Which invention do these pictures stand for?
78800.e: A fastener with lots of interlocking teeth is pulled up on a pair of trousers. The zip in its modern form was developed around 1913 by Gideon Sundback.
78800.m: In a zip, lots of little teeth lock into each other.

78801.q: Which famous experiment do these pictures stand for?
78801.e: A light ball and a dark ball fall from a tower at the same time. According to tradition, Galileo Galilei showed in Pisa that heavy and light bodies fall equally fast without air resistance.
78801.m: Without air resistance, heavy and light bodies fall equally fast.

78802.q: Which famous experiment do these pictures stand for?
78802.e: A kite in a thunderstorm and a key on the string: in 1752 Benjamin Franklin wanted to show this way that lightning is an electrical discharge. The experiment was life-threatening.
78802.m: Franklin’s kite experiment was meant to show that lightning is electrical.

78803.q: Which famous experiment do these pictures stand for?
78803.e: Sun, temple, ruler and Earth: around 240 BC, Eratosthenes compared the lengths of shadows at noon in two places in Egypt and used them to calculate the Earth’s circumference amazingly accurately.
78803.m: Eratosthenes calculated the Earth’s circumference using shadow angles and geometry.

78804.q: Which famous experiment do these pictures stand for?
78804.e: A monastery, plants and green and yellow peas lead to heredity. The monk Gregor Mendel crossed peas in the monastery garden in Brno and so found the basic rules of inheritance.
78804.m: Gregor Mendel discovered the basic rules of inheritance using peas.

78805.q: Which famous experiment do these pictures stand for?
78805.e: A swan, a glass flask and crossed-out microbes: around 1860 Louis Pasteur used flasks with a curved neck to show that no microbes arise by themselves in boiled broth.
78805.m: With the swan-neck flask, Pasteur disproved the spontaneous generation of microbes.

78806.q: Which famous experiment do these pictures stand for?
78806.e: Two hemispheres from which the air has been pumped out cannot be pulled apart even by teams of horses. Otto von Guericke used them in the 17th century to demonstrate the force of air pressure.
78806.m: The Magdeburg hemispheres showed the enormous force of air pressure.

78807.q: Which famous experiment do these pictures stand for?
78807.e: Light from a lamp passes through two narrow slits (pause symbol) and creates a striped pattern like a zebra. Around 1802 Thomas Young used it to show that light has wave properties.
78807.m: The double-slit experiment shows the wave nature of light with a striped pattern.

78808.q: Which famous experiment do these pictures stand for?
78808.e: A child sits in front of a sweet and waits; whoever waits gets two. From the late 1960s Walter Mischel studied delayed gratification this way at Stanford University.
78808.m: The marshmallow test studies whether children can wait for a bigger reward.

78809.q: Which famous experiment do these pictures stand for?
78809.e: An elephant looks at itself in the mirror and notices a red spot on itself. In the mirror test, developed by Gordon Gallup in 1970, scientists check whether animals recognise themselves in a mirror.
78809.m: The mirror test checks whether an animal recognises itself in a mirror.

78810.q: Which constellation do these pictures stand for?
78810.e: A bear and stars forming a cart: seven bright stars in the constellation of the Great Bear form the well-known shape of the Plough.
78810.m: The Plough is part of the constellation of the Great Bear.

78811.q: Which constellation do these pictures stand for?
78811.e: A small teddy bear, a star and a compass pointing north: the Pole Star is the brightest star in the Little Bear and points almost exactly north.
78811.m: The Pole Star belongs to the Little Bear and points north.

78812.q: Which constellation do these pictures stand for?
78812.e: A man with a belt of three stars in the winter sky: the constellation of Orion represents a hunter and is easy to recognise by the three stars of his belt.
78812.m: You can recognise Orion in the winter sky by his three belt stars.

78813.q: Which constellation do these pictures stand for?
78813.e: A queen with a crown on a throne between stars: in Greek legend Cassiopeia was a vain queen; her constellation has the shape of a W.
78813.m: The constellation of Cassiopeia has the shape of a W.

78814.q: Which constellation do these pictures stand for?
78814.e: A scorpion with a red heart among the stars: the red giant star Antares is seen as the heart of the scorpion.
78814.m: The red star Antares forms the heart of the scorpion.

78815.q: Which constellation do these pictures stand for?
78815.e: Two men side by side and two stars stand for the bright stars Castor and Pollux. They form the heads of the constellation Gemini, the twins.
78815.m: Castor and Pollux are the brightest stars of Gemini.

78816.q: Which constellation do these pictures stand for?
78816.e: A cross of stars, an arrow pointing south and the southern hemisphere: the Southern Cross can only be seen well from the southern hemisphere and appears on several national flags, such as Australia’s.
78816.m: The Southern Cross is a well-known constellation of the southern hemisphere.

78817.q: Which constellation do these pictures stand for?
78817.e: A bull with a reddish glowing eye: the red giant star Aldebaran forms the eye of the bull; the Pleiades lie in the same constellation.
78817.m: The red star Aldebaran is seen as the eye of the bull.

78818.q: Which constellation do these pictures stand for?
78818.e: A dog and an especially brightly twinkling star at the top: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, belongs to Canis Major, the Great Dog.
78818.m: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky and belongs to Canis Major.

78819.q: Which record-breaking place do these pictures stand for?
78819.e: The sea, arrows pointing down and a hole in the Pacific region show the deepest point of the oceans. The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench lies about 11,000 metres below sea level.
78819.m: The Mariana Trench in the Pacific is the deepest point of the world’s oceans.

78820.q: Which record holder do these pictures stand for?
78820.e: A whale, a ruler and a gold medal: the blue whale grows up to about 30 metres long and is the largest known animal that has ever lived.
78820.m: The blue whale is the largest known animal in the history of the Earth.

78821.q: Which record holder do these pictures stand for?
78821.e: A big cat, a cloud of dust and a gold medal stand for the fastest land animal. A cheetah briefly reaches about 100 kilometres per hour in a sprint.
78821.m: The cheetah is the fastest land animal on Earth.

78822.q: Which world record holder do these pictures stand for?
78822.e: A lightning bolt, a runner, the number 100 and a stopwatch: in Berlin in 2009, Usain Bolt ran the 100 metres in 9.58 seconds, a world record (as of 2026).
78822.m: Usain Bolt holds the 100 metres world record with 9.58 seconds.

78823.q: Which record-breaking building do these pictures stand for?
78823.e: Tower blocks, an arrow pointing up, clouds and a gold medal stand for the tallest building in the world. The Burj Khalifa in Dubai is 828 metres high (as of 2026).
78823.m: At 828 metres, the Burj Khalifa in Dubai is the tallest building in the world (as of 2026).

78824.q: Which record holder do these pictures stand for?
78824.e: A bird of prey dives down as fast as an arrow. In a dive the peregrine falcon reaches over 300 kilometres per hour and is therefore considered the fastest animal in the world.
78824.m: In a dive, the peregrine falcon is the fastest animal in the world.

78825.q: Which record-breaking lake do these pictures stand for?
78825.e: A lake, an arrow pointing down, water and a gold medal: at about 1,640 metres, Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake on Earth.
78825.m: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake on Earth.

78826.q: Which record holder do these pictures stand for?
78826.e: A conifer, a ruler and an arrow pointing up stand for the tallest tree. The coast redwood “Hyperion” in California is about 116 metres tall.
78826.m: The coast redwood is the tallest tree species in the world.

78827.q: Which record holder do these pictures stand for?
78827.e: A bird, a bee and the gesture for tiny: the bee hummingbird from Cuba is only about 5 to 6 centimetres long and the smallest bird in the world.
78827.m: The bee hummingbird from Cuba is the smallest bird in the world.

78828.q: What is a variety of beech with dark red leaves called?
78828.e: The copper beech is a special form of the common beech. Its leaves are dark red, which is why people like to plant it in parks.
78828.m: The copper beech has dark red leaves.

78829.q: What does the bark of a common beech feel like?
78829.e: The common beech has smooth, silver-grey bark. Even old beeches usually stay smooth on the trunk.
78829.m: Beech bark is smooth and grey.

78830.q: What is beech wood often used for?
78830.e: Beech wood is hard and easy to work. Chairs, tables and wooden toys are made from it.
78830.m: Furniture is often made from beech wood.

78832.q: What does the edge of a beech leaf look like?
78832.e: The beech leaf is oval and has a smooth, slightly wavy edge. There are often fine hairs along the edge.
78832.m: The beech leaf has a slightly wavy edge.

78833.q: Which animal likes to eat beechnuts in autumn?
78833.e: Beechnuts are rich in fat and nutrients. Squirrels, mice and birds like to eat them.

78834.q: What do the buds of the common beech look like in winter?
78834.e: The common beech has long, narrow, pointed buds. You can recognise it by them even in winter.
78834.m: Beech buds are long and pointed.

78835.q: Which group of trees does the common beech belong to?
78835.e: The common beech has broad leaves and loses them in autumn. That makes it a broadleaf tree.
78835.m: The common beech is a broadleaf tree.

78836.q: Why is a beech wood often quite dark in summer?
a: The canopy of leaves is very dense.
Beeches only grow in the shadow of mountains.
78836.e: The many beech leaves form a dense roof. Only a little sunlight reaches the ground.
78836.m: In a beech wood a dense canopy keeps out the light.

78837.q: Which forest animal really likes to eat acorns in autumn?
78837.e: Acorns are nourishing. Wild boar search for them on the forest floor in autumn.

78838.q: Why is the pedunculate oak called that?
a: Its acorns hang on long stalks.
It has a very thin trunk.
Broom handles are made from it.
78838.e: A peduncle is a stalk. On the pedunculate oak the acorns hang on long stalks, while the leaves have only very short stalks.
78838.m: The pedunculate oak carries its acorns on long stalks.

78839.q: When do the ripe acorns fall from the tree?
78839.e: Acorns ripen in late summer. In autumn they fall to the ground.
78839.m: Acorns fall from the tree in autumn.

78840.q: What does an acorn sit in?
78840.e: The bottom of the acorn sits in a little cup. It looks a bit like a little hat.
78840.m: The acorn sits in a little cup.

78841.q: What are the little balls sometimes found on oak leaves called?
78841.e: A small wasp, the gall wasp, lays its eggs in the oak leaf. The leaf forms a ball around them, the oak gall.
78841.m: Oak galls are caused by gall wasps.

78842.q: Which bird hides acorns as a store and so helps to plant new oaks?
78842.e: The jay buries lots of acorns in autumn. It does not find some of them again, and young oaks grow from them.
78842.m: The jay buries acorns and so plants oaks.

78843.q: What does the bark of an old oak look like?
78843.e: Young oaks have smooth bark. On old oaks the bark becomes thick and gets deep furrows.
78843.m: Old oaks have thick, furrowed bark.

78844.q: Which wood are wine barrels often made of?
78844.e: Oak wood is hard, heavy and dense. That is why it is good for barrels.
78844.m: Wine barrels are often made of oak.

78845.q: Why is an old oak so important for animals?
a: A great many insect species live on it.
It has no leaves to get in the way.
Only fish live in its roots.
It keeps all animals out of the forest.
78845.e: Hundreds of different insect species live on oaks. Many birds in turn feed on them.
78845.m: An oak is a home for a great many insects.

78846.q: Roughly how long is a spruce cone?
78846.e: Spruce cones are long and narrow, about 10 to 15 cm long. They are brown when ripe.
78846.m: Spruce cones are about as long as a hand.

78847.q: What oozes out when the bark of a spruce is damaged?
78847.e: The spruce seals wounds with sticky resin. This protects it from fungi and insects.

78848.q: What shape is the crown of a young spruce?
78848.e: Young spruces have a narrow, pointed crown. It looks like a cone.
78848.m: The spruce has a pointed crown.

78849.q: Where does the spruce grow naturally in Switzerland, above all?
78849.e: Naturally, the spruce grows mainly in mountain forests. In the Central Plateau it was often planted by people.
78849.m: The spruce is naturally a mountain tree.

78850.q: How are the needles arranged on a spruce twig?
a: Only on top of the twig
78850.e: On the spruce, the needles stand singly all round the twig. This makes it look like a bottle brush.
78850.m: Spruce needles sit all round the twig.

78851.q: What is spruce wood very often used for?
78851.e: Spruce wood is light and grows back quickly. It is used for roof beams, boards and also paper.
78851.m: Houses are often built with spruce wood.

78852.q: Why are spruces easily blown over in strong storms?
a: They have no roots at all.
78852.e: The roots of the spruce spread out flat under the ground like a plate. That is why the wind can blow them over more easily.

78853.q: Which small beetle can harm many spruces?
78853.e: The bark beetle bores tunnels under the bark. Weakened spruces can die from it.
78853.m: The bark beetle harms many spruces.

78854.q: What do you often find on the forest floor under a spruce?
78854.e: The spruce drops its ripe cones whole. That is why there are often lots of cones under it.
78854.m: Whole cones often lie under spruces.

78855.q: Roughly how tall can a silver fir grow?
78855.e: The silver fir is one of the tallest trees in our forests. It often grows 30 to 50 metres tall.
78855.m: Silver firs can grow very tall.

78856.q: Why do you hardly ever find whole cones under a silver fir?
a: The cones fall apart up on the tree
The cones stay on the tree for ever
The cones melt in the rain
78856.e: Silver fir cones stand upright on the branches. They fall apart up there into single scales, so hardly any whole cones fall down.
78856.m: Fir cones fall apart on the tree.

78857.q: What does the crown of an old silver fir often look like?
a: Flat on top like a stork’s nest
78857.e: On old silver firs the top hardly grows any more. The crown becomes flat on top and looks like a stork’s nest.
78857.m: Old silver firs often have a flat crown.

78858.q: What do the needles of the silver fir feel like?
78858.e: The needles of the silver fir are flat and blunt or slightly notched at the tip. That is why they do not prick.

78859.q: Where does the silver fir get its name from?
78859.e: The bark of the silver fir is light grey to whitish. That is where the name comes from.
78859.m: The silver fir has pale bark.

78860.q: Why does the silver fir usually stay firmly in the ground in a storm?
a: It has a deep main root.
78860.e: The silver fir forms a strong root that goes deep into the ground. This lets it hold on well in a storm.
78860.m: The silver fir is anchored with deep roots.

78861.q: Which animal likes to nibble young silver firs?
78861.e: Roe deer like to eat the buds and shoots of young firs. That is why young trees are sometimes protected with fences.
78861.m: Roe deer like nibbling young firs.

78862.q: How are the needles of the silver fir arranged on the twig?
a: Flat to the left and right
78862.e: The needles of the silver fir stand flat on both sides of the twig like a comb. They are said to be parted.
78862.m: Fir needles stand flat to the left and right of the twig.

78863.q: How do the fruits of the sycamore fly from the tree?
78863.e: The fruits of the sycamore have a wing. As they fall they spin like a little helicopter and fly a long way.
78863.m: Maple fruits fly like little propellers.

78864.q: What does a sycamore leaf look like?
a: Like a hand with five lobes
Like a feather with many leaflets
78864.e: The sycamore leaf is large and has five lobes. It looks like an open hand.
78864.m: The maple leaf looks like a hand.

78865.q: Which country’s flag has a maple leaf on it?
78865.e: The flag of Canada has a red maple leaf. Different maple species grow in Canada from the ones here.
78865.m: Canada has a maple leaf on its flag.

78866.q: What happens to the bark of an old sycamore?
78866.e: On older sycamores the bark comes off in flat scales. Lighter patches can be seen underneath.

78867.q: Where does the sycamore grow well in Switzerland?
a: Even high up in the mountains
78867.e: The sycamore grows well in mountain forests. You often find it as a single large tree on alpine pastures.
78867.m: The sycamore likes growing in the mountains.

78868.q: For which musical instrument is maple wood often used?
78868.e: Maple wood is pale, hard and beautifully patterned. The back of a violin is often made of maple.
78868.m: Violins are often made with maple wood.

78869.q: What colour are sycamore leaves usually in autumn?
78869.e: In autumn sycamore leaves turn yellow to golden yellow. Then they fall off.
78869.m: Sycamore leaves turn yellow in autumn.

78871.q: How many needles grow together from one point on the Scots pine?
78871.e: On the Scots pine, two needles always grow together. At the bottom they are held by a small sheath.
78871.m: The Scots pine has needles in pairs.

78872.q: What colour is the bark at the top of a Scots pine’s trunk?
78872.e: At the top of the trunk and on the branches the bark of the Scots pine is fox-red to orange. Lower down it becomes grey and cracked.
78872.m: The Scots pine has orange-red bark at the top.

78874.q: Which well-known forest in Valais consists mainly of pines?
78874.e: The Pfyn forest lies in Valais between Leuk and Sierre. It is one of the largest pine forests in the Alps.
78874.m: The Pfyn forest in Valais is a large pine forest.

78875.q: Where does the Scots pine grow especially often?
78875.e: The Scots pine is undemanding. It grows even where the soil is dry, sandy or stony.
78875.m: The Scots pine copes with dry soil.

78876.q: How much light does the Scots pine need?
78876.e: The Scots pine is a light-loving tree. It grows badly in the shade of other trees.
78876.m: The Scots pine needs a lot of light.

78877.q: What do the needles of the Scots pine often look like?
78877.e: The needles of the Scots pine are blue-green, about 4 to 7 cm long and often slightly twisted.
78877.m: Scots pine needles are often slightly twisted.

78878.q: What does an older Scots pine often look like?
a: A long bare trunk with the crown at the top
Branches right down to the ground
Crown at the bottom, trunk at the top
78878.e: Old Scots pines lose their lower branches. That is why they have a long bare trunk and an umbrella-like crown at the top.
78878.m: Old Scots pines carry their crown high up.

78879.q: What is different about the larch compared with our other conifers?
a: It loses its needles in autumn.
It has no needles at all.
78879.e: The larch is a conifer that sheds all its needles in autumn. New needles grow in spring.
78879.m: The larch loses its needles in autumn.

78880.q: What colour are larches in autumn?
78880.e: Before the larch sheds its needles, they turn golden yellow. In autumn whole mountainsides glow yellow.
78880.m: Larches turn golden yellow in autumn.

78881.q: How do the needles grow on the short shoots of the larch?
78881.e: On the short shoots of the larch, many needles grow together in a bunch. A bunch has about 20 to 40 needles.

78882.q: What do larch needles feel like?
78882.e: Larch needles are thin and soft. They do not prick.

78883.q: Where in Switzerland do especially many larches grow?
a: In Lake Constance, in the water
78883.e: The larch likes to grow high in the mountains, for example in Valais and the Engadine. It grows up to the tree line.
78883.m: Many larches grow in the Alps.

78884.q: Why do people like to build balconies from larch wood?
a: It stands up well to wind and weather
78884.e: Larch wood contains a lot of resin and is very durable. That is why it lasts a long time outdoors.

78885.q: Roughly how big are larch cones?
78885.e: Larch cones are small and egg-shaped. They often stay hanging on the tree for years.

78886.q: What colour are the new larch needles in spring?
78886.e: In spring the larches put out fresh, light green needles. They glow softly in the mountain forest.
78886.m: In spring larch needles are light green.

78887.q: What colour is the bark of a young birch?
78887.e: The birch has white bark. That makes it instantly recognisable.

78888.q: The silver birch is also called the “weeping birch”. Why?
a: Its roots hang in the air.
78888.e: On the silver birch the fine, thin twigs hang downwards. They move even in a light wind.
78888.m: The silver birch has drooping twigs.

78889.q: Roughly what shape is a birch leaf?
78889.e: The leaf of the silver birch is roughly triangular to diamond-shaped. The edge is finely toothed.
78889.m: The birch leaf is roughly triangular.

78890.q: What does the birch do on an open, empty area?
a: It is one of the first trees to grow there.
It waits until all the other trees are there.
78890.e: Birches are pioneer trees. Their light seeds fly a long way, and they grow quickly on open ground.
78890.m: The birch is often the first to grow on open ground.

78891.q: What are the long, hanging flowers of the birch called?
78891.e: The birch flowers in spring with long flower clusters. They are called catkins.
78891.m: The flowers of the birch are called catkins.

78892.q: Why do some people sneeze in spring because of the birch?
78892.e: In spring birches release a lot of pollen into the air. Some people are allergic to it and get hay fever.
78892.m: Birch pollen can cause hay fever.

78893.e: Birch seeds are tiny and have little wings. The wind carries them far away.
78893.m: The wind carries birch seeds away.

78894.q: What does the bark at the bottom of an old birch’s trunk look like?
78894.e: On old birches the bark at the bottom of the trunk gets dark, deep cracks. Further up it stays white.
78894.m: Old birches are black and cracked at the bottom.

78895.q: What colour are the buds of the ash in winter?
78895.e: The ash has striking black buds. You can recognise it by them even in winter without leaves.

78896.q: How is an ash leaf built?
a: Like a hand with five fingers
78896.e: The ash leaf is pinnate. It is made of several small leaflets on a shared stalk.
78896.m: The ash leaf is made of many leaflets.

78897.q: What has been threatening many ash trees in Switzerland for some years?
78897.e: An introduced fungus causes ash dieback. Many ash trees fall ill from it and die.
78897.m: A fungal disease is making many ash trees ill.

78898.q: What is the tough wood of the ash used for?
78898.e: Ash wood is hard and bends without breaking. That is why handles for hammers and spades are made from it.
78898.m: Tool handles are often made of ash wood.

78899.q: What often hangs in bunches on the ash in winter?
78899.e: Ash fruits have a long wing. They often hang in bunches on the tree all winter.
78899.m: Ash fruits hang in bunches on the tree.

78900.q: Where does the ash especially like to grow?
a: By streams and on damp soil
78900.e: The ash likes damp, nutrient-rich soils. You often find it along streams and rivers.
78900.m: The ash likes growing in damp places.

78901.q: When does the ash get its leaves?
78901.e: The ash puts out its leaves late, often not until May. Other broadleaf trees are already green by then.
78901.m: The ash gets its leaves late.

78902.q: Which tree is the world tree in old Norse legends?
78902.e: In the Norse legends the world tree is called Yggdrasil. It is described as a giant ash.
78902.m: The world tree of the Norse legends is an ash.

78903.q: Roughly how tall can an ash grow?
78903.e: The common ash is a large tree. It can grow up to about 40 metres tall.
78903.m: Ash trees can grow very tall.

78904.q: What must you definitely know about the yew?
a: It is as sweet as sugar.
78904.e: Almost all parts of the yew are poisonous, especially the needles and seeds. You must not eat any of it.

78905.q: What colour are the berry-like fruits of the yew?
78905.e: The yew’s seed sits in a red, fleshy cup. The seed inside is very poisonous.
78905.m: The yew has red, berry-like fruits.

78906.q: How fast does the yew grow?
78906.e: The yew grows very slowly. But it can live to a great age.

78907.q: What does the yew not have, even though it is a conifer?
78907.e: The yew does not form cones. Its seed sits singly in a red cup.

78908.q: For which animal are yew twigs especially dangerous?
78908.e: Just a few yew twigs can kill a horse. That is why yews are not planted next to horse pastures.
78908.m: Yews are very dangerous for horses.

78909.q: What was yew wood often used for in the past?
78909.e: Yew wood is very tough and flexible. People were already making bows from it in the Stone Age.
78909.m: In the past bows were made of yew wood.

78910.q: Where can the yew still grow well?
78910.e: The yew needs little light. It even grows in the shade under large trees.
78910.m: The yew grows in the shade too.

78911.q: Where do you often see yews outside the forest?
a: As a hedge in the garden
78911.e: Yews are easy to trim and stay green all year. That is why they are often planted as hedges in gardens and parks.
78911.m: Yews often grow as garden hedges.

78912.q: Which tree is the hornbeam closely related to?
78912.e: Although its leaves look like beech leaves, the hornbeam belongs to the birch family. It is not closely related to the common beech.
78912.m: The hornbeam is related to the birch.

78914.q: What does the trunk of a hornbeam often look like?
78914.e: The trunk of the hornbeam is not round, but has bulges and grooves. It looks as if it had muscles.
78914.m: The hornbeam trunk looks as if it were covered in muscles.

78915.q: What is the edge of a hornbeam leaf like?
78915.e: The hornbeam leaf has a finely, doubly toothed edge. The leaf surface looks as if it were pleated.
78915.m: The hornbeam leaf has a toothed edge.

78916.q: Why do people like to plant hornbeams as a hedge?
a: It copes well with being cut.
It only grows for one summer.
78916.e: The hornbeam sprouts again and again after being cut. That is why it is a popular hedge plant.
78916.m: The hornbeam is easy to trim.

78917.e: Hornbeam wood is one of the hardest woods in our forests. In the past cogwheels and tools were made from it.

78918.q: How do the fruits of the hornbeam get away from the tree?
a: They fly in the wind with a wing
They float away in the stream
78918.e: Each small hornbeam fruit hangs from a wing. The wind carries them away from the tree.
78918.m: Hornbeam fruits fly with the wind.

78919.q: What does a trimmed hornbeam hedge often do in winter?
78919.e: Many hornbeam hedges only lose their brown leaves in spring. So they stay thick even in winter.
78919.m: Hornbeam hedges often keep their dry leaves in winter.

78920.q: How many needles grow together from one spot on a Swiss stone pine?
78920.e: On the Swiss stone pine, five needles always grow in one bundle. That makes it easy to recognise.
78920.m: The Swiss stone pine has its needles in fives.

78921.q: What is inside the cones of the Swiss stone pine?
78921.e: Swiss stone pine cones contain nourishing seeds. They are called pine nuts, and you can eat them.
78921.m: Swiss stone pine cones contain edible little nuts.

78922.q: Which bird hides the nuts of the Swiss stone pine and so helps new trees to grow?
78922.e: In autumn the spotted nutcracker hides lots of pine nuts in the ground. Young trees grow from the stores it forgets.
78922.m: The spotted nutcracker plants Swiss stone pines.

78923.q: How old can a Swiss stone pine get?
78923.e: The Swiss stone pine grows slowly and can live a very long time. Some trees are several hundred to about 1000 years old.
78923.m: Swiss stone pines can get very old.

78924.q: What is the wood of the Swiss stone pine especially known for?
78924.e: Swiss stone pine wood smells nice and keeps its scent for a long time. People even fill pillows with its shavings.
78924.m: Swiss stone pine wood smells lovely.

78925.q: What can the Swiss stone pine cope with especially well?
78925.e: The Swiss stone pine grows where winters are very long and cold. It copes well with severe cold.
78925.m: The Swiss stone pine can stand severe cold.

a: a room panelled with Swiss stone pine
78926.e: In an Arvenstube the walls and ceiling are covered with Swiss stone pine wood. Rooms like this are common in houses in the Grisons.
78926.m: An Arvenstube is panelled with Swiss stone pine wood.

78927.q: What is another name for the Swiss stone pine?
78927.e: The Swiss stone pine is also called the arolla pine. In Switzerland people mostly call it “Arve”.
78927.m: The Swiss stone pine is also called the arolla pine.

78928.q: What does a researcher do when she observes something?
78928.e: Observing means looking and listening very carefully. That way you notice even small things.

78929.q: Which tool lets you see small animals such as ants bigger?
78929.e: A magnifying glass has a curved glass. It makes small things look bigger.
78929.m: With a magnifying glass you see small things bigger.

78930.q: Which device do you use to watch birds that are far away?
78930.e: Binoculars bring faraway things closer. That way you can watch birds without disturbing them.
78930.m: With binoculars you see faraway things.

78931.q: Which device lets you see tiny things that you cannot see with the naked eye?
78931.e: A microscope magnifies very strongly. With it you can see cells in a leaf, for example.

78932.q: What is the best way to behave when watching animals in the forest?
78932.e: Wild animals get frightened by noise and run away. If you are quiet, you can watch them better.

78933.q: Which scientist became famous for watching wild chimpanzees for many years?
78933.e: From 1960 Jane Goodall watched chimpanzees in Tanzania. She saw, for example, that chimpanzees use tools.
78933.m: Jane Goodall studied chimpanzees by watching them.

78934.q: Which sense do you use to notice whether a bird is singing?
78934.e: You notice a bird’s song with your ears. Listening is part of observing too.
78934.m: You also observe with your ears.

78935.q: What did Galileo Galilei discover in 1610 when he observed Jupiter with his telescope?
78935.e: Next to Jupiter, Galileo saw four small points of light that moved. They were moons circling Jupiter.
78935.m: By observing, Galileo discovered moons around Jupiter.

78936.q: What does research usually begin with?
78936.e: At the start there is a question you want to answer. Then you think about how to find the answer.

78937.q: Which of these questions can you investigate with an experiment?
a: Does ice melt faster in the sun?
What is my best friend’s name?
Do I prefer dogs or cats?
78937.e: Whether ice melts faster in the sun can be tried out and measured. The other questions are about taste or about knowledge of yourself.
78937.m: A good research question can be tested.

78938.q: Which question word do you use to ask for the reason for something?
78938.e: Researchers often want to know why something is the way it is. With “why” you ask for the reason.

78939.q: What should a good research question be like?
78939.e: A clear question shows exactly what you want to find out. Then you know what you have to investigate.
78939.m: A good research question is clear.

78940.q: Lea asks: “Do cress seeds grow without water too?” What is that?
78940.e: Lea wants to find out something she can test. That is why her question is a research question.
78940.m: A research question wants to find something out.

78941.q: Where do many research questions come from?
a: from the luck of the draw
78941.e: If you wonder about something, you ask questions. Many good research questions come from wondering.

78942.q: Which question is too big for a single experiment?
a: How does the whole universe work?
Does a ball roll faster down a slope?
Does an apple float in water?
Does sticky tape stick to glass?
78942.e: Many people have been studying how the whole universe works for centuries. Small questions, on the other hand, can be tested with a simple experiment.
78942.m: Small questions can be tested with an experiment.

78943.q: What do you usually do next after the research question?
78943.e: After the question you think about what the answer could be. You then test this guess.
78943.m: After the question comes the guess.

a: an idea of what might happen
78944.e: A guess is a thought about what the answer might be. You only know whether it is right after testing it.
78944.m: A guess is an idea that you test.

78945.q: What technical word do researchers use for a guess?
78945.e: A hypothesis is a guess that can be tested with experiments or observations.
78945.m: In research a guess is called a hypothesis.

a: I think the stone will sink.
The stone is called a pebble.
78946.e: “I think” shows that you do not know it for sure yet. That is a guess.
78946.m: A guess often begins with “I think”.

78947.q: What happens if a guess turns out to be wrong?
78947.e: A wrong guess also brings new knowledge. Afterwards you know how it is not.
78947.m: A wrong guess also brings knowledge.

78948.q: When do you write down a guess?
78948.e: You write the guess down beforehand. Afterwards you can compare honestly whether it is right.
78948.m: Write the guess down before the experiment.

78949.q: How do you find out whether a guess is right?
a: You test it with an experiment.
You ask a friend what she thinks.
You wish for it very hard.
You take a vote in class.
78949.e: You test a guess by trying things out, observing or measuring. Asking, voting or wishing proves nothing.

78950.q: Nino guesses: “The plant grows better in the light than in the dark.” What should he do now?
78950.e: Nino can put one plant in the light and one in the dark. That way he tests his guess.
78950.m: You test a guess by trying it out.

78951.q: Where do you get good ideas for a guess?
78951.e: A good guess is based on knowledge and earlier observations. If you know, for example, that plants need water, you can make a good guess about what happens without water.
78951.m: A good guess builds on knowledge.

78952.q: What is a planned trial in research called?
78952.e: In an experiment you try something out in a planned way. That is how you test a guess.
78952.m: A planned trial is called an experiment.

78953.q: What is part of a safe experiment?
a: lighting a fire on your own
78953.e: You can hurt yourself in some experiments. That is why you ask an adult first.
78953.m: In experiments, ask an adult first.

78954.q: Mia puts an apple, a stone and a cork into water. What does she find out?
78954.e: Mia tries out which things float in water and which sink. That is a simple experiment.
78954.m: With water you can try out what floats.

78955.q: What do you get ready before an experiment?
78955.e: Before the experiment you get all the materials ready. That way you can work calmly and tidily.
78955.m: Get the materials ready before the experiment.

78956.q: You want to test whether a plant grows better with more light. How do you make the experiment with two plants fair?
a: Only the light is different, everything else is the same
Everything is different: light, water and soil
Both plants get exactly the same amount of light
78956.e: Fair means you change only one thing, here the light. Water, soil and pot stay the same. If one plant grows better, you then know for sure that it is because of the light.
78956.m: In a fair test you change only one thing.

78957.q: Where do many researchers work on experiments?
78957.e: A laboratory is a room with equipment for experiments. Researchers can work calmly and safely there.
78957.m: Researchers often do experiments in the laboratory.

78958.q: Why do researchers wear safety goggles in some experiments?
78958.e: In experiments something can splash. Safety goggles protect the eyes from this.

78959.q: What do you do with your workspace after an experiment?
78959.e: After the experiment you tidy up and clean the materials. That way everything is ready for next time.

78960.q: What do you do when you compare?
a: You look for things that are the same and different.
78960.e: When comparing, you look at two or more things. You look for what is the same and what is different.
78960.m: Comparing means finding similarities and differences.

78961.q: One snail crawls 10 cm, another 15 cm. How much further did the second one crawl?
78961.e: You work out 15 cm minus 10 cm. That makes 5 cm.
78961.m: When comparing lengths, you work out the difference.

78962.q: What is the best thing to use to compare which of two stones is heavier?
78962.e: Scales show the weight. That way you can see exactly which stone is heavier.

78963.q: Two pots of cress are on the windowsill. One is watered, one is not. What are you comparing?
78963.e: The only difference is the water. That way you can see what effect watering has.
78963.m: You compare what a difference causes.

78964.q: What is the tool called that you can use to compare the length of two leaves?
78964.e: With a ruler you measure lengths in centimetres. Then you can compare the numbers.
78964.m: You measure lengths with a ruler.

78965.q: An ice cube melts in 10 minutes in the sun and in 25 minutes in the shade. Where does it melt faster?
78965.e: 10 minutes is less than 25 minutes. So the ice cube melts faster in the sun.
78965.m: Ice melts faster in the sun.

78966.q: What helps you compare lots of measurements clearly?
78966.e: In a table the values are set out neatly side by side. That way you see differences quickly.

78967.q: Why do you measure when comparing, instead of just estimating?
78967.e: Estimates can be misleading. With a measuring device you get exact numbers.
78967.m: Measuring is more precise than estimating.

78968.q: What is a research diary for?
78968.e: In a research diary you record what you have observed and tried out. That way you do not forget anything.
78968.m: You write observations in the research diary.

78969.q: What do you add to every entry in the research diary?
78969.e: With the date you know later when you observed something. That way you can follow changes.

78970.q: Which naturalist travelled around the world on the ship “Beagle” and filled many notebooks?
78970.e: Charles Darwin travelled around the world on the ship “Beagle”. He wrote his observations carefully in notebooks.
78970.m: Darwin wrote his observations in notebooks.

78971.q: Why do you write down observations straight away?
a: so that you do not forget anything
78971.e: Your memory can play tricks on you. If you write things down straight away, you have exact notes later.

78972.q: Besides text, what else can you put in a research diary?
a: tear pages out and throw them away
78972.e: In a research diary, drawings, tables and stuck-in finds also help. Anything that records the research is allowed.
78972.m: You can also draw in the research diary.

78973.q: Ella watches a bean for 14 days. What helps her most in her research diary?
a: only writing on the last day
only the colour of the notebook
78973.e: With daily entries Ella can see exactly how the bean grows day by day.

78974.q: What do you write honestly in the research diary if an experiment goes wrong?
78974.e: A research diary must be honest. Experiments that went wrong belong in it too.
78974.m: Write honestly in the research diary what happened.

78975.q: Where can you find out later exactly how an experiment was done?
78975.e: The research diary says which materials and which steps were used. That way you can repeat the experiment.
78975.m: The research diary says how an experiment went.

78976.e: The result is what comes out at the end of the experiment. You write it down carefully.
78976.m: The result is what you have found out.

78977.q: What do you compare the result with at the end?
78977.e: You check whether the result matches the guess. That way you know whether the guess was right.
78977.m: At the end you compare the result with the guess.

78978.q: How can you show a result to others well?
78978.e: On a poster you can show the question, the experiment and the result. That way others understand quickly.
78978.m: A poster shows a result well.

78979.q: What do researchers do so that others find out about their results?
a: They write them down for everyone.
They hide them in the cellar.
78979.e: Researchers write down their results and tell others about them. That way everyone can learn from them.
78979.m: Researchers share their results with others.

78980.q: What does a bar chart show?
a: numbers as bars of different heights
78980.e: In a bar chart each number is a bar. The bigger the number, the taller the bar.
78980.m: A bar chart shows numbers as bars.

78981.q: What should you do if a result is surprising?
78981.e: Surprising results are often especially exciting. You write them down carefully and check them.

78982.q: Kim counts 3 ladybirds on Monday and 5 on Tuesday. How many is that altogether?
78982.e: You work out 3 plus 5. That makes 8 ladybirds.
78982.m: You can add up results from several days.

78983.q: What does the result of an experiment answer?
78983.e: You do an experiment to answer a question. The result gives the answer to it.
78983.m: The result answers the research question.

78984.q: Why do researchers repeat an experiment?
a: to check whether the result is right
because they have forgotten the result
78984.e: Something can go wrong the first time. If the same thing comes out in several trials, the result is more reliable.
78984.m: Repeating shows whether a result is right.

78985.q: A paper aeroplane flies 3 m once, 5 m once and 4 m once. What is the best thing to do?
a: throw it more often and compare
78985.e: The throws went different distances. If you throw more often, you can see better how far the plane usually flies.
78985.m: Several trials give a more accurate picture.

78986.q: How should you repeat an experiment?
a: exactly the same as the first time
completely differently from the first time
78986.e: Only if you do everything the same can you compare the results. Otherwise you do not know why something is different.
78986.m: When repeating, do everything the same.

78987.q: Why is it good when other researchers also repeat an experiment?
a: That way you see whether the result is really right.
That way the experiment becomes secret.
That way everyone gets a present.
That way it becomes more expensive.
78987.e: If other researchers find out the same thing, you can trust the result more.
78987.m: Others check results by repeating them.

78988.q: What is needed so that others can repeat an experiment?
78988.e: Only someone who knows exactly how the experiment went can repeat it. That is why you describe every step.
78988.m: An exact description makes experiments repeatable.

78989.q: Tom measures the length of a leaf three times: 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm. What does that show?
a: The leaf is growing very fast.
78989.e: If every measurement gives the same result, you can trust the measurement.
78989.m: Equal measurements show a reliable measurement.

78990.q: What can a single experiment without repetition easily show?
78990.e: In a single experiment chance can play a part. Only repetitions make a result more certain.
78990.m: A single experiment can depend on chance.

78991.q: Why do you count birds in the garden on several days?
a: because every day can be different
78991.e: On one day lots of birds come, on another only a few. Several counts give a better picture.
78991.m: Several counts give a better picture.

78992.q: What do researchers often say about mistakes?
78992.e: A mistake shows what does not work. You can learn from it and do better.

78993.q: Which medicine did Alexander Fleming discover because a mould grew on a forgotten dish?
78993.e: In 1928 Fleming saw that a mould killed bacteria on his dish. That is how he discovered penicillin.
78993.m: Penicillin was discovered by a lucky accident.

78994.q: What do you do if an experiment does not work?
a: find out why and try again
78994.e: You think about what went wrong. Then you change something and try again.
78994.m: If something does not work, you look for the reason.

78995.q: Which rays did Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discover rather by chance in 1895?
78995.e: During an experiment Röntgen noticed a strange glow. That is how he discovered rays that are used today to look inside the body.

78996.q: Why do you also write mistakes in the research diary?
a: so that you do not repeat them
so that the notebook gets fuller
78996.e: If you write down your mistakes, you know next time what to watch out for.
78996.m: Mistakes you write down, you do not make again.

78997.e: With a measuring error the measured number is not quite right. For example, you held the ruler at an angle.
78997.m: With a measuring error the number is inaccurate.

78998.q: What can an experiment show that does not bring the expected result?
a: That the guess was perhaps wrong
That the experiment is completely worthless
That you should never do research again
That laws of nature sometimes do not apply
78998.e: An unexpected result brings new questions. You check the guess or the experiment again, and sometimes a great discovery is made this way.
78998.m: Unexpected results lead to new questions.

78999.q: Roughly how many attempts did Thomas Edison need for a good light bulb?
78999.e: Edison and his team tried out very many materials for the filament. Many attempts failed until one worked.
78999.m: Good inventions often need many attempts.

79000.q: Which quality often makes people do research?
79000.e: If you are curious, you want to understand things. That is why research often begins with curiosity.

79001.q: Which famous physicist said of himself that he was only “passionately curious”?
79001.e: In a letter in 1952 Albert Einstein wrote that he had no special talents. He was only passionately curious.

79002.q: How can you tell that a child is curious?
79002.e: Curious children want to know a lot. That is why they often ask “Why?” and “How?”.
79002.m: Curious people ask lots of questions.

79003.q: What is the name of a NASA vehicle that drives around on Mars doing research?
79003.e: The rover Curiosity landed on Mars in 2012. Its name means the wish to find things out.
79003.m: The Mars rover is named Curiosity.

79004.q: What can you do if you are curious about animals?
a: just sit quietly in your room
79004.e: If you watch animals in the forest, you learn a lot about them. Books and museums also help you discover things.

79005.q: What does a curious person do if they do not know an answer?
a: look it up or try it out
79005.e: Curious people look for answers. They read up, ask others or try things out themselves.
79005.m: Curious people look for answers themselves.

79006.q: Where can you see stuffed animals, rocks and dinosaur bones?
79006.e: A natural history museum shows animals, plants, rocks and fossils. There are such museums in Bern, Basel and Geneva, for example.
79006.m: In the natural history museum you can discover nature.

79007.q: Where in Switzerland can you try out experiments yourself?
a: at the Federal Palace in Bern
79007.e: The Swiss Science Center Technorama in Winterthur has hundreds of hands-on experiments to touch and try out.
79007.m: At the Technorama you can try out experiments yourself.

79008.q: Why do researchers often work in a team?
79008.e: In a team each person brings their knowledge and ideas. That way bigger questions can be solved.
79008.m: In a team you achieve more.

79009.q: Near which Swiss city is the large research centre CERN?
79009.e: CERN is near Geneva on the border with France. Thousands of researchers from many countries work together there.

79010.q: Which pair of researchers discovered the substance radium together?
79010.e: Marie and Pierre Curie researched together and discovered new substances such as radium. For this they shared a Nobel Prize in 1903.
79010.m: Marie and Pierre Curie researched together.

79011.q: What is important in a research team?
79011.e: In a team you listen to each other and discuss ideas. That way better solutions come about.
79011.m: In a team you listen to each other.

79012.q: How can a class research team share out the work well?
a: Everyone does the same thing at the same time.
79012.e: One child measures, one writes things down, one fetches materials. That way everyone helps.
79012.m: In a research team every child has a task.

79013.q: What does a team do if two members have different guesses?
79013.e: Different ideas are valuable. With an experiment the team can find out which guess is right.

79014.q: Who often belongs to a team that builds a space probe?
79014.e: A space probe needs engineers, physicists, computer scientists and many more. Each person can do something different.

79015.q: In what did the Swiss Auguste Piccard and a helper become the first to fly into the stratosphere in 1931?
79015.e: In 1931 Auguste Piccard and his helper Paul Kipfer went up in a gas balloon with a pressurised cabin. The two reached a height of almost 16 km.
79015.m: In 1931 Auguste Piccard and a helper flew into the stratosphere.

79016.q: Why do researchers draw plants and animals?
a: because they do not like pens
79016.e: When you draw, you have to look closely at every detail. You discover a lot that you would otherwise miss.

79017.q: Which painter and naturalist drew more than 300 years ago how caterpillars turn into butterflies?
79017.e: Maria Sibylla Merian lived from 1647 to 1717. She watched caterpillars and drew their transformation into butterflies very precisely.
79017.m: Maria Sibylla Merian drew the transformation of butterflies.

79018.q: Which famous artist and inventor filled many notebooks with drawings of machines and birds?
79018.e: Leonardo da Vinci drew flying machines, birds’ wings and the human body. His notebooks are famous.
79018.m: Leonardo da Vinci researched with drawings.

79019.q: What do you write next to a scientific drawing?
79019.e: You label the parts, for example leaf, stem and root. That way everyone understands the drawing.

79020.q: What should a scientific drawing be like?
a: accurate and as true to life as possible
79020.e: A scientific drawing shows what something really looks like. You do not add anything made up.
79020.m: A scientific drawing is accurate and true to life.

79021.q: Which tool helps you draw a small insect accurately?
79021.e: In a bug viewer the insect sits safely and looks bigger. That way you can draw it well.
79021.m: With a bug viewer you can draw insects well.

79022.q: What do you write next to a drawing so that people know the real size?
a: how big the thing really is
79022.e: A drawing can be bigger or smaller than the original. That is why you note the real size, for example 2 cm.
79022.m: Note the real size next to the drawing.

79023.q: What is the best thing to draw scientific sketches with?
79023.e: With a sharp pencil you can draw fine lines. You can rub out mistakes.
79023.m: Draw scientific sketches with a sharp pencil.

79024.q: You put a glass over a burning candle. Why does the flame soon go out?
a: It runs out of fresh air.
79024.e: A flame needs oxygen from the air. Under the glass it runs short, and the flame goes out.

79025.e: A measurement is the number a measuring device shows, for example 12 cm. Many measurements together make up the result.
79025.m: A measurement is a measured number.

79026.q: At which university in Zurich do many research teams work?
79026.e: ETH Zurich is a federal technical university. Many teams from all over the world do research there.
79026.m: Many teams do research at ETH Zurich.

79027.q: One tree is 12 m tall, another 21 m. Which one is taller?
79027.e: 21 is bigger than 12. So the tree that is 21 m is taller, by 9 m.

79028.q: Which organ in your head do you think with?
79028.e: The brain is in the head. We use it to think, learn and remember.

79029.q: How many eyes does a person have?
79029.e: A person has two eyes. With two eyes you can judge well how far away something is.

79030.q: What is the front part of the head with the eyes, nose and mouth called?
79030.e: The eyes, nose and mouth are at the front of the head. This part is called the face.
79030.m: The eyes, nose and mouth are part of the face.

79031.q: Where on the body are the ears?
a: On the sides of the head
At the front of the neck
At the back of the neck
79031.e: The ears sit on the left and right of the head. That way we can hear which direction a sound comes from.
79031.m: The ears sit on the sides of the head.

79032.q: What grows on top of most people's heads?
79032.e: Hair grows on the head. It protects a little against sun and cold.

79033.q: What is the back of the neck called?
79033.e: At the back of the neck is the nape. Strong muscles there hold up the head.
79033.m: The back of the neck is called the nape.

79034.q: What do you wear round your neck in winter against the cold?
79034.e: A scarf keeps your neck warm. You wrap it round once or twice.
79034.m: A scarf keeps your neck warm.

79035.q: Which organ in your neck do you need for speaking and singing?
79035.e: The vocal cords sit in the voice box. When air flows past them, they vibrate and make sounds.
79035.m: The voice box makes our voice.

79036.q: Which piece of jewellery do you wear round your neck?
79036.e: You put a necklace round your neck. Often a small pendant hangs from it.
79036.m: You wear a necklace round your neck.

a: Between the neck and the arm
Between the knee and the foot
Between the hand and the finger
Between the tummy and the leg
79037.e: The shoulder is at the top side of the trunk. That is where the arm begins.
79037.m: The shoulder is between the neck and the arm.

79038.q: What is the flat bone at the back of the shoulder called?
79038.e: The shoulder blade is a flat, triangular bone. It is at the back of the upper back.
79038.m: The shoulder blade is at the back of the shoulder.

79039.q: Which joint can you move furthest in a circle?
79039.e: The shoulder joint is the most movable joint in the body. That is why you can swing your arm in a big circle.
79039.m: The shoulder is our most movable joint.

79040.q: What do you often show when you shrug your shoulders?
a: That you do not know something
79040.e: When you shrug, you lift your shoulders briefly. That way you show without words: I don't know.
79040.m: A shrug often means “I don't know”.

79041.q: Which part of the arm is directly below the shoulder?
79041.e: The upper arm reaches from the shoulder to the elbow. There is a long bone inside it.
79041.m: The upper arm begins below the shoulder.

79042.q: What does it mean to “give someone the cold shoulder”?
a: To give them a friendly hug
79042.e: The saying means that you deliberately ignore someone. You turn away from them, so to speak.
79042.m: If you give someone the cold shoulder, you ignore them.

79043.q: In which sport do players wear big shoulder pads?
79043.e: In ice hockey, players often crash into each other. Shoulder pads under the shirt cushion the knocks.
79043.m: Ice hockey players protect their shoulders with pads.

79044.q: Which joint is in the middle of the arm?
79044.e: The elbow is roughly in the middle of the arm. That is where you can bend the arm.
79044.m: The elbow is in the middle of the arm.

79045.q: What can you do with your elbow?
79045.e: With the elbow joint you bend your arm and straighten it again. That way you can, for example, bring a spoon to your mouth.
79045.m: We bend our arm with the elbow.

79047.q: What was the “ell” used for in the past?
79047.e: The ell used to be a measure of length. It was roughly the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.
79047.m: The ell used to be a measure of length.

79048.q: Where is the “funny bone” that tingles so much when you knock it?
79048.e: At the elbow, a nerve lies just under the skin. If you knock it there, it tingles all the way into your fingers.
79048.m: The funny bone is at the elbow.

79049.q: Roughly how does the elbow move when you bend it?
79049.e: The elbow folds the arm mainly in one direction, like a door on its hinge. In addition, the forearm can twist.
79049.m: The elbow folds like a hinge.

79050.q: What does it mean to “elbow your way” forward?
a: To push ahead without caring about others
79050.e: If you elbow your way forward, you push in front and only think of yourself. It is a saying.
79050.m: If you elbow your way forward, you push ahead without caring about others.

79051.q: Which joint connects the hand to the forearm?
79051.e: The wrist is where the hand begins. It makes the hand movable.
79051.m: The wrist connects the hand and forearm.

79052.q: Where do you usually wear a wristwatch?
79052.e: A wristwatch goes round the wrist. That way you can check the time quickly.
79052.m: You wear a wristwatch on your wrist.

79053.q: How many wrist bones does one hand have?
79053.e: There are eight small wrist bones in the wrist. They are arranged in two rows.

79054.q: Which joint do people especially often injure when they fall onto an outstretched hand?
79054.e: When people fall, they often catch themselves with their hands. This puts a lot of strain on the wrist, and it can break.
79054.m: When you fall onto your hand, the wrist often suffers.

79055.q: Which part of the arm is between the wrist and the elbow?
79055.e: The forearm reaches from the wrist to the elbow. There are two bones inside it.
79055.m: The forearm is between the wrist and the elbow.

79056.q: What do you mainly move when you wave your hand?
79056.e: When you wave, your hand tips back and forth. The wrist makes this movement possible.
79056.m: When you wave, your wrist moves.

79057.q: Which is the largest joint in the human body?
79057.e: The knee joint is the largest human joint. It carries a lot of weight when you walk and jump.
79057.m: The knee is our largest joint.

79058.q: What do you wear on your knees for protection when inline skating?
79058.e: Knee pads have hard shells. They protect your knees if you fall.
79058.m: Knee pads protect your knees when skating.

79059.q: What is the soft area at the back of the knee called?
79059.e: At the back of the knee there is a small hollow. It is called the hollow of the knee.
79059.m: The hollow of the knee is at the back of the knee.

79060.q: How do many babies get about before they can walk?
a: They crawl on their hands and knees
79060.e: Many babies crawl first. They support themselves on their hands and knees.
79060.m: Babies crawl on their hands and knees.

a: At the back of the foot
At the front by the toes
At the top of the knee
At the bottom of the hand
79061.e: The heel is the round back part of the foot. A lot of weight rests on it.
79061.m: The heel is at the back of the foot.

79062.q: What is the largest bone in the foot called?
79062.e: The heel bone is the largest bone of the foot. It forms the heel.
79062.m: The heel bone is the largest foot bone.

79063.q: Which part of the foot usually touches the ground first when you walk normally?
79063.e: When you walk, you usually put your foot down heel first. Then it rolls forwards.
79063.m: When you walk, the heel touches down first.

79064.q: Where do you often get a blister in new, stiff shoes?
79064.e: New shoes often rub at the back of the heel. The rubbing causes a blister.
79064.m: New shoes often rub on the heel.

79065.q: What is the raised part of the shoe under the heel called?
79065.e: The heel of a shoe is the raised back part of the sole. It sits exactly under your heel.
79065.m: The shoe's heel sits under your heel.

79066.q: What does it mean to be “hot on someone's heels”?
79066.e: If you are hot on someone's heels, you follow them very closely. The saying fits, for example, a chase.
79066.m: If you are on someone's heels, you follow them closely.

79067.q: What forms on your heels if you often go barefoot?
79067.e: The skin on the heel gets thicker and harder from pressure. This hard layer is called hard skin.
79067.m: Hard skin forms on your heels.

79068.q: How many toes does a person have altogether on both feet?
79068.e: Each foot has five toes. Together that makes ten toes.

79069.q: What is the thickest toe on the foot called?
79069.e: The big toe is the thickest and strongest. When you walk, you push off with it.
79069.m: The big toe is the thickest.

79070.e: Right on the outside of the foot is the little toe. It is easy to stub on table legs.
79070.m: The smallest toe is right on the outside.

79071.q: How is it best to cut toenails?
79071.e: Toenails cut straight across are less likely to grow into the skin. That prevents pain.

79072.q: What do your toes especially help you with?
79072.e: When you stand and walk, your toes press against the ground. That way they help you not to fall over.

79073.q: In which dance do dancers in pointe shoes stand on the tips of their toes?
79073.e: In ballet there is pointe work. The dancers stand on the tips of their toes in special shoes.
79073.m: In ballet you dance on the tips of your toes.

79074.q: How many toes does a chicken usually have on one foot?
79074.e: Most chickens have four toes on each foot. A few breeds have five.
79074.m: A chicken usually has four toes on each foot.

a: At the front in the middle of the tummy
79075.e: The belly button is on the front of the tummy, roughly in the middle. Almost everyone has one.
79075.m: The belly button is on the front of the tummy.

79076.q: What actually is the belly button?
79076.e: The belly button is a scar that everyone gets as a baby. After that it stays for life.
79076.m: The belly button is a scar.

79077.q: What sometimes collects in the belly button?
79077.e: Fine fibres come off clothes. They can collect in the belly button as fluff.
79077.m: Fluff sometimes collects in the belly button.

79078.q: Which of these animals also has a navel?
79078.e: Mammals such as dogs have a navel, often well hidden under their fur. Chickens, frogs and fish hatch from eggs and do not have a navel like this.
79078.m: Mammals such as dogs have a navel too.

79079.q: How is it best to clean your belly button?
a: Gently with water in the shower
79079.e: In the shower you can wash your belly button gently with water and a little soap. Then dry it well.
79079.m: You wash your belly button gently in the shower.

79080.q: What do people mean when they say a place is “the navel of the world”?
a: It is the most important centre
79080.e: The navel is in the middle of the tummy. That is why a particularly important place is also called “the navel of the world”.

79081.q: Which long organ lies in many loops behind the belly button?
79081.e: The gut lies in the tummy in many coils. It digests the food further.
79081.m: The gut lies behind the belly button.

79082.q: Which part of the body is at the front between the belly button and the neck?
79082.e: Above the tummy comes the chest and then the neck. The heart and lungs are in the chest.
79082.m: The chest is above the tummy.
