80169.e: In a clicky ballpoint pen, a small spring pushes the refill back in when you click again.
80169.m: A ballpoint pen often has a small spring inside.

80170.q: Why do some bikes have springs?
80170.e: Suspension absorbs the bumps from stones and roots. So the ride is smoother, especially off-road.
80170.m: Springs on a bike absorb bumps.

80171.q: What squeezes a clothes peg shut?
80171.e: In the middle of a clothes peg there is a small metal spring. It presses the two halves together and holds the washing in place.
80171.m: A spring keeps a clothes peg closed.

80172.q: What do you tighten when you wind up a mechanical clock?
80172.e: A mechanical clock has a coiled spring inside. Winding tightens it, and it then drives the clock.
80172.m: A tightened spring drives a mechanical clock.

80173.q: What do we use to move our body?
80173.e: Muscles contract and so move the bones. Without muscles we could not move.

80174.q: Which force drives an ordinary bike without a motor?
80174.e: When you ride a bike, your legs push the pedals. The force for this comes from your muscles.
80174.m: A bike without a motor runs on muscle power.

80175.q: What are most muscles attached to?
a: The skin on the soles of the feet
80175.e: Muscles are attached to the bones by tendons. When a muscle contracts, it pulls on the bone and moves it.

80176.q: What can you feel in your muscles the day after doing a lot more sport than usual?
80176.e: After unusual effort, your muscles often ache. This is called muscle soreness, and it goes away after a few days.
80176.m: Sore muscles come after unusual effort.

80177.e: The biceps is a muscle at the front of the upper arm. It bends the arm, for example when you lift a bag.
80177.m: The biceps is on the upper arm.

80178.q: Which muscle works all your life without a break?
80178.e: The heart is a muscle. It pumps blood through the body day and night.
80178.m: The heart is a muscle that never takes a break.

80179.q: What is the largest muscle in the human body called?
80179.e: The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the body. It helps with walking, climbing stairs and standing up.
80179.m: The largest muscle is the gluteus maximus.

80180.q: Roughly how many muscles does a person have?
80180.e: A person has over 600 muscles. They work together when we move.

80181.q: What happens to a billiard ball that is lying still when another ball hits it?
a: It jumps up to the ceiling
80181.e: In the collision, the rolling ball passes on part of its momentum. The ball that was still starts to roll.
80181.m: A push can set a ball lying still in motion.

80182.q: Which way does a marble roll when you push it with your finger?
a: In the direction of the push
80182.e: A marble moves in the direction you push it. The direction of the force decides the direction of the movement.
80182.m: A marble rolls in the direction of the push.

80183.q: In which sport do you push a heavy metal ball as far as possible?
80183.e: In shot put, you push the ball powerfully forwards from your neck. Whoever puts it furthest wins.
80183.m: In shot put you push a ball a long way.

80184.q: In which Swiss tradition do you throw a heavy stone as far as possible?
80184.e: Stone putting (Steinstossen) is an old Swiss competition. The heavy Unspunnen stone is famous.
80184.m: Stone putting is a Swiss tradition.

80185.q: What knocks over the pins in skittles?
a: The push of the rolling ball
80185.e: The ball rolls against the pins and knocks into them. This makes the pins fall over.
80185.m: In skittles, the ball knocks over the pins.

80186.q: What protects your head from a hard knock when cycling?
80186.e: A cycle helmet has a thick layer of foam inside. In a fall, it absorbs the knock and protects the head.
80186.m: A cycle helmet protects your head from a knock.

80187.q: In a car, what absorbs the impact for the people in an accident?
80187.e: In an accident, the airbag inflates in a flash. It slows the body gently and absorbs the impact.
80187.m: The airbag absorbs the impact in an accident.

80188.q: What do you feel when another car bumps into yours on the dodgems?
80188.e: In the collision, a force acts on the car. You feel it as a strong jolt.
80188.m: In a collision you feel a jolt.

80189.q: What do you give a football when you kick it?
80189.e: When you kick, your foot touches the ball only very briefly. This short, strong push sends the ball flying.
80189.m: When you kick a ball, it gets a push.

80190.q: What is the throwing sport with a flat, round disc called?
80190.e: In the discus, you spin round and fling a flat, round disc of wood and metal a long way.
80190.m: In the discus you throw a round disc.

80191.q: What shape is the path of a ball that is thrown a long way?
80191.e: The ball first flies up and forwards and then falls down again. This makes an arc.
80191.m: A thrown ball flies in an arc.

80192.q: What helps you throw a ball further?
a: Throwing it with your eyes shut
80192.e: The more force you use when throwing, the faster the ball sets off. That is why it flies further.
80192.m: With more force, a ball flies further.

80193.q: Which object is thrown in athletics?
80193.e: In the javelin, you throw a long, pointed spear as far as possible.
80193.m: The javelin is thrown in athletics.

80194.q: What is special about a boomerang?
a: It can fly back to the thrower
80194.e: A boomerang has a special curved shape. Thrown correctly, it flies in an arc and comes back.

80195.q: In which game do you throw a ball into a high basket?
80195.e: In basketball, you throw the ball into a basket that hangs high up on a board. Every basket scores points.
80195.m: In basketball you throw the ball into the basket.

80196.q: In which game do you throw balls as close as possible to a small target ball?
80196.e: In boccia, you throw large balls. Whoever is closest to the small target ball gets points.
80196.m: In boccia you throw balls close to the target ball.

80197.q: Why do you swing your arm far back when throwing?
80197.e: When you swing far back, your arm can speed up the ball over a longer distance. So the ball gets more momentum.
80197.m: Swinging far back gives more momentum when throwing.

80198.q: What happens to modelling clay when you press it hard?
80198.e: Modelling clay changes shape when you press it and then stays in the new shape. That is why it is good for making figures.
80198.m: Modelling clay stays in the shape you press it into.

80199.q: What happens to a rubber ball when you squeeze it and let go again?
80199.e: The rubber ball only changes shape for a moment when squeezed. Afterwards it goes back to its round shape.
80199.m: A rubber ball becomes round again after being squeezed.

80200.q: What happens to an empty drinks can when you stand on it?
80200.e: The thin metal of the can cannot hold the weight. It bends and stays crushed.
80200.m: An empty can gets crushed under pressure.

80201.q: What happens to a glass bottle that falls onto a stone floor?
a: It bounces back like a ball
80201.e: Glass is hard but brittle. In a hard impact, it does not bend; it breaks.
80201.m: Glass breaks easily in a hard impact.

80202.q: What happens to loose snow when you squeeze it together firmly?
80202.e: When you squeeze, the snow is pressed together. It changes shape and becomes firm and hard.
80202.m: Snow becomes firm when squeezed together.

80203.q: Why can you see your footprints in wet sand?
a: Your foot presses the sand down
The wind blows the prints in
80203.e: The weight of your body presses the sand under your foot together. The sand keeps this shape as a print.
80203.m: Footprints form because your foot changes the shape of the sand.

80204.q: What happens to a thin branch when a bird sits on it?
80204.e: The bird's weight presses on the branch. That is why it bends down a little.
80204.m: A weight can bend a branch.

80205.q: What is it called when an object does not return to its old shape after being pressed?
80205.e: With permanent deformation, the object stays in its new shape. A dent in a bike mudguard is an example.
80205.m: A permanent deformation does not go away by itself.

80206.q: Where on a force meter do you read how big the force is?
80206.e: A force meter has a scale with numbers printed on it. A marker there shows how big the force is.
80206.m: You read the value on the scale.

80207.q: What is inside a simple force meter?
80207.e: A simple force meter contains a spring. The harder you pull, the further it stretches.
80207.m: There is a spring inside a force meter.

80208.q: What does a force meter show when you pull on it harder?
80208.e: When you pull harder, the spring stretches further. The pointer moves to a higher value.
80208.m: More force gives a higher value on the force meter.

80209.q: Roughly how many newtons does a force meter show when one kilogram hangs from it?
80209.e: On Earth, one kilogram pulls down with about 10 newtons. More exactly, it is about 9.8 newtons.
80209.m: One kilogram pulls down with about 10 newtons.

80210.q: What does a force meter show when nothing hangs from it and nobody is pulling?
80210.e: Without a force, the spring is not stretched. So the pointer is at zero.
80210.m: Without a force, the force meter shows zero.

80211.q: Which device works like a force meter and shows how heavy a suitcase is?
80211.e: A spring balance also has a spring inside. If you hang the suitcase from it, you can read how heavy it is.
80211.m: A spring balance works with a spring.

80212.q: What can happen if you put far too much load on a force meter?
a: The force meter starts to glow
80212.e: Every force meter has a maximum value. If you pull harder, the spring gets overstretched and no longer measures correctly.
80212.m: You should not overload a force meter.

80213.q: In which direction does the full moon rise?
80213.e: Like the Sun, the Moon rises roughly in the east and sets in the west. This is because the Earth spins.
80213.m: The Moon rises in the east.

80214.q: Roughly when does the full moon rise?
80214.e: The full moon is opposite the Sun. That is why it rises when the Sun sets.
80214.m: The full moon rises in the evening when the Sun sets.

80215.q: At full moon, what is roughly between the Sun and the Moon?
80215.e: At full moon, the Sun, the Earth and the Moon are almost in a line, with the Earth in the middle. So we see the whole lit side of the Moon.
80215.m: At full moon the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon.

80216.q: At which phase of the Moon can there be a lunar eclipse?
80216.e: In a lunar eclipse, the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. That can only happen when the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, so at full moon.
80216.m: A lunar eclipse only happens at full moon.

80217.q: On a clear night, how long can you see the full moon?
80217.e: The full moon rises in the evening and does not set until the morning. That is why it is in the sky all night.
80217.m: The full moon shines all night.

80218.q: What do you call a second full moon in the same calendar month?
80218.e: The Moon is not actually blue at all. It is just a name.
80218.m: A second full moon in the same month is called a blue moon.

80219.q: The full moon often looks huge just above the horizon. Is it really bigger then?
80219.e: The Moon is no bigger at the horizon than high in the sky. Our brain tricks us because we compare it with houses and trees.
80219.m: The huge Moon at the horizon is a trick of our brain.

80220.q: What colour is the full moon often during a total lunar eclipse?
80220.e: A little sunlight is bent by the Earth's atmosphere and falls on the Moon with a reddish colour. That is why people also speak of a “blood moon”.
80220.m: During a total lunar eclipse the Moon glows reddish.

80221.q: Which animal is said to howl at the full moon?
80221.e: In stories, wolves howl at the Moon. In reality, wolves howl to communicate with their pack, not because of the Moon.
80221.m: Wolves howl to talk to their pack.

80222.q: What does the Moon look like to us at new moon?
80222.e: At new moon, the side of the Moon facing us is not lit by the Sun. That is why we can hardly see it.
80222.m: At new moon the Moon is almost invisible to us.

80223.q: Why can't you see the Moon at new moon?
a: Its bright side faces away from us
It is made of ice then
80223.e: The Sun always lights up one half of the Moon. At new moon, exactly this bright half faces away from the Earth.
80223.m: At new moon the lit side of the Moon faces away from us.

80224.q: Roughly where is the Moon at new moon?
a: Between the Earth and the Sun
80224.e: At new moon, the Moon is on the side of the Earth where the Sun is too. So from here it is near the Sun in the sky.
80224.m: At new moon the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun.

80225.q: At which phase of the Moon can there be a solar eclipse?
80225.e: For the Moon to cover the Sun, it has to be between the Earth and the Sun. That is only the case at new moon.
80225.m: A solar eclipse only happens at new moon.

80226.q: What can you see in the evening sky a few days after new moon?
80226.e: After new moon, a little more of the Moon is lit every day. At first you see a thin crescent shortly after sunset.
80226.m: After new moon, a thin crescent appears first.

80227.q: When is the Moon in the sky at new moon?
a: During the day, together with the Sun
Only in the middle of the night
80227.e: The new moon rises and sets at about the same time as the Sun. So it is in the sky during the day, but you cannot see it in the bright sunlight.
80227.m: The new moon travels across the sky with the Sun during the day.

80228.q: Why is a night with a new moon good for watching the stars?
a: Because the sky is especially dark
Because there are more stars then
Because the stars are coloured then
80228.e: Without moonlight, the night sky is darker. Then you can see faint stars and the Milky Way better.
80228.m: On new moon nights you see the stars best.

80229.q: How is the new moon drawn in many calendars?
80229.e: In calendars, a dark, filled-in circle stands for the new moon. An empty circle means full moon.
80229.m: In a calendar, the new moon is a dark dot.

80230.q: Roughly how many days after new moon do you see the first half moon?
80230.e: It takes the Moon about a week from new moon until half of its disc is lit.
80230.m: About a week after new moon there is a half moon.

80231.q: Which side of the waxing half moon is bright in Switzerland?
80231.e: In the northern hemisphere, so here too, the waxing Moon is bright on the right. With the waning Moon it is the left side.
80231.m: Here the waxing Moon is bright on the right.

80232.q: What comes after the waxing half moon?
80232.e: After the waxing half moon, the bright part gets bigger and bigger. After about a week it is full moon.
80232.m: The full moon follows the waxing half moon.

a: You see less of it every day
It gets lighter in weight every day
It flies away from the Earth
80233.e: After full moon, the lit part we see gets a little smaller every day. But the Moon itself stays the same size.
80233.m: With a waning Moon we see less bright surface every day.

80234.q: How much of the Moon's disc is bright at half moon?
80234.e: At half moon we see a bright half and a dark half. That is where its name comes from.
80234.m: At half moon, half of the disc is bright.

80235.q: What else is the waxing half moon called?
80235.e: The Moon has then completed a quarter of its journey around the Earth. That is why this phase is also called the “first quarter”.
80235.m: The waxing half moon is also called the first quarter.

80236.q: When can you see the waning half moon well in the sky?
80236.e: The waning half moon rises at about midnight. That is why you see it in the second half of the night and in the morning.
80236.m: You see the waning half moon in the morning.

80237.q: When can you see the waxing half moon well in the sky?
80237.e: The waxing half moon rises at about midday and sets at about midnight. That is why you see it in the afternoon and evening.
80237.m: You see the waxing half moon in the evening.

80238.q: How did most craters on the Moon form?
a: From impacts of chunks of rock
80238.e: Many chunks of rock from space have crashed onto the Moon. The impacts made round holes, the craters. Because the Moon has no air, they last a long time.
80238.m: Moon craters are marks of impacts from space.

80239.q: Why do craters on the Moon last so long?
a: There is no wind and no water there
The craters are made of metal
80239.e: On Earth, craters are slowly worn away by wind, rain and rivers. On the Moon there is none of that.
80239.m: Without wind and water, Moon craters last a very long time.

80240.q: What does a crater on the Moon look like?
80240.e: A crater is a round hollow with a raised rim. It looks like a bowl in the ground.
80240.m: A crater is a round hollow with a rim.

80241.q: What can you already use to see Moon craters well from Earth?
80241.e: Even simple binoculars show many craters on the Moon. With a telescope you can see even more details.
80241.m: With binoculars you can spot Moon craters.

80242.q: What can you see around some young Moon craters at full moon?
80242.e: Bright rays spread out from some young craters such as Tycho. You can see them well at full moon.
80242.m: Some Moon craters have bright rays.

80243.q: Who are many Moon craters named after?
80243.e: Many craters have the names of well-known scientists, for example Copernicus or Kepler.
80243.m: Many Moon craters are named after scientists.

80244.q: At which phase of the Moon can you see craters especially well through binoculars, because they cast long shadows?
80244.e: At half moon, sunlight falls at a slant on many craters. Then their rims cast long shadows and you can see them clearly.
80244.m: Craters are best seen at half moon.

80245.q: Why does the Moon have many more visible craters than the Earth?
a: It has no protective layer of air
It is bigger than the Earth
It is closer to the Sun
80245.e: Small chunks burn up in the Earth's atmosphere before they reach the ground. The Moon has no such atmosphere.
80245.m: The atmosphere protects the Earth from many small chunks.

80246.q: What is the face of the “man in the Moon” made of?
a: Clouds in front of the Moon
80246.e: There are light and dark areas on the Moon. To many people, the dark patches look like a face.
80246.m: The man in the Moon is made of dark patches.

80247.q: Why do we always see the man in the Moon the same way?
a: The Moon always shows us the same side
The patches move along with it
80247.e: The Moon turns exactly once around itself while it goes once around the Earth. That is why we always see the same side of it.
80247.m: The Moon always shows the Earth the same side.

80248.q: Which animal do many people in China or Japan see in the patches on the Moon?
80248.e: In East Asia people tell of the rabbit in the Moon. To people there, the dark patches look like a rabbit.
80248.m: In East Asia people see a rabbit in the Moon.

80249.q: What is the side of the Moon called that you can never see from Earth?
a: The far side of the Moon
The near side of the Moon
80249.e: Because the Moon always shows us the same side, the other side stays hidden. It is called the far side of the Moon.
80249.m: You can never see the far side of the Moon from Earth.

80250.q: Is the side of the Moon that we never see always dark?
a: It is only bright at full moon
80250.e: This side is lit by the Sun just as much as the side facing us. At new moon it is even completely lit.
80250.m: The side of the Moon we never see also gets sunlight.

80251.q: Why do we see faces in the Moon, in clouds or in plug sockets?
a: Our brain likes to look for faces
80251.e: Our brain recognises faces very quickly. That is why we often see them even where there are none.
80251.m: Our brain likes to spot faces everywhere.

80252.q: When can you see the whole face of the man in the Moon?
80252.e: Only at full moon is the whole side facing us lit up. Then you see all the dark patches at the same time.
80252.m: You see the whole face in the Moon at full moon.

80253.q: How do people in Australia see the man in the Moon?
a: Exactly the same as we do
Not at all, only the far side
80253.e: In the southern hemisphere, people look at the Moon from the other side of the Earth. That is why the face in the Moon is upside down for them.
80253.m: In the southern hemisphere the face in the Moon is upside down.

80254.q: Is there water in the seas on the Moon?
80254.e: The lunar seas are flat, dry areas of rock. No real water flows there.
80254.m: There is no water in the seas on the Moon.

80255.q: What did the seas on the Moon form from?
80255.e: A very long time ago, liquid lava flowed from inside the Moon into large basins. It hardened and today forms the dark plains.
80255.m: The seas on the Moon are made of hardened lava.

80256.q: Why are the dark plains on the Moon called “seas”?
a: Early scientists thought they were water
80256.e: A few hundred years ago, scientists thought the dark patches were seas. The name has stuck, even though there is no water there.
80256.m: The seas on the Moon got their name from an old mistake.

80257.q: In which lunar sea did Apollo 11 land?
80257.e: The first crewed Moon landing took place in the Sea of Tranquillity in 1969. The plain was flat and good for landing.
80257.m: Apollo 11 landed in the Sea of Tranquillity.

80258.q: What is the largest dark area on the Moon called?
80258.e: The Ocean of Storms is so big that it is called not just a sea but an ocean. It lies on the left side of the Moon.
80258.m: The largest lunar sea is called the Ocean of Storms.

80259.q: What colour are the seas on the Moon when seen from Earth?
80259.e: The rock of the lunar seas is darker than that of the bright highlands. That is why they look dark grey.
80259.m: The seas on the Moon look dark grey.

80260.q: Which Latin word is used for a sea on the Moon?
80260.e: “Mare” is Latin for sea. The Sea of Tranquillity, for example, is called “Mare Tranquillitatis”.
80260.m: A sea on the Moon is called mare in Latin.

80261.q: Do the seas on the Moon have more or fewer craters than the bright areas?
80261.e: The lunar seas are younger than the bright highlands. So fewer chunks have had time to hit them, and they look smoother.
80261.m: The seas on the Moon are smoother and have fewer craters.
